To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) we develop a new approach to the problem of computing approximately maximum s−t flows in undirected graphs; (b) this approach is based on electrical flows; (c) the algorithm we develop is the fastest known algorithm to compute a (1-ϵ)-approximately maximum s−t flow, with running time ~O(m n1/3ϵ−11/3); (d) we also obtain the fastest known algorithm, with running time~O(m + n4
(1) electrical flow problems can be solved in nearly-linear time; and (2) this approach leads to the fastest known algorithms for computing approximately maximum flows and approximately minimum cuts.

(1) electrical flow problems are useful in designing faster algorithms for computing approximate maximum flows and minimum cuts, (2) solving electrical flow problems can be reduced to solving systems of linear equations in Laplacian matrices, and (3) solving systems of linear equation in Laplacian matrix can be done faster than previously known.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of finding an approximately maximum s - t flow in a capaci- tated, undirected graph, where the flow is required to satisfy a set of linear flow conservation constraints.
the problem of computing a (1-δ)-approximately maximum s - t flow in a capacited, undirected graph, where 0< δ< 1.

the following questions: Given a graph with nonnegative capacities on the edges, how do we efficiently compute the maximum flow? How can we compute a minimum cut? What are the connections between electrical flows, Laplacian systems, the maximum flow problem, and the minimum cut problem?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach is the first to break through the barrier of √m, and it is the first to achieve a near-linear time algorithm.
our algorithm is faster than Goldberg and Rao's for any ε < 1/2, and is slower for ε ≥ 1/2.

we have improved the dependence on m and ε in the running time for computing approximately maximum flows and approximately minimum s−t cuts in undirected graphs from O(mnε−2) to O(mε−3/2) and from O(mn1/2ε−2)to O(mε−2) respectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the first time, we have an algorithm that runs in time nearly-linear in m and n for computing approximately maximum/minimum flows/cuts.
the dependence on m has been improved from √n to n<sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub>, and the dependence on n has been improved from n<sup>3</sup>/<sub2</sub> to n<sup>(4/3)</sup>.

we have developed an algorithm for computing approximately max-flow and approximately min-cut in undirected graphs in nearly-linear time, and the dependence on n is better than the previous algorithm by Goldberg and Rao.
The main takeaway from our work is that
electrical flows are useful for designing algorithms for flow and cut problems.
electrical flows can be a useful tool for approximating combinatorial flows.

electrical flow problems, and in particular the Laplacian system of linear equations that arise in their analysis, can be efficiently used to compute approximately optimum s-t flows and cuts in undirected graphs.
